subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Toyota Production System
description: A quick win: understand The Toyota Production System.

hook.text: Toyota didn't beat Detroit with better designs. It beat them with a better factory system.

buildup.text: Engineer Taiichi Ohno developed 'just-in-time' production—parts arrive exactly when needed, no stockpiles.

discovery.text: Workers could stop the entire line if they spotted a defect. Quality was everyone's job.

twist.text: American factories optimized for speed. Toyota optimized for zero waste—and ended up faster anyway.

climax.text: The Toyota Production System became the basis for 'lean manufacturing' used worldwide today.

punchline.text: Toyota's real product wasn't cars—it was the system.

quiz.question: What is 'just-in-time' production?
options: Shipping cars the day they're ordered

details.summary: The Toyota Production System pioneered lean manufacturing by eliminating waste, empowering workers to stop the line for defects, and delivering exactly what customers needed with minimal inventory.
details.whyItMatters: TPS revolutionized global manufacturing beyond cars. Its principles of continuous improvement, just-in-time delivery, and respect for workers became the foundation of modern lean management.
takeaways: Just-in-time reduces inventory to only what is needed right now
Any worker can stop the production line to fix a quality issue
Kaizen means continuous incremental improvement by everyone

faq.question: How is TPS different from Ford's assembly line?
faq.answer: Ford focused on volume through standardization. TPS focuses on flexibility and quality, building different models on the same line with zero defects and minimal waste, adapting to demand in real time.

faq.question: Do non-automotive companies use the Toyota Production System?
faq.answer: Widely. Hospitals, software companies, banks, and restaurants have adopted lean principles from TPS. The methodology has become one of the most influential management philosophies of the 20th century.
